gives: The date of death, from the press
Four notices say 13 MAY 1827, two of them within four days of it. Connolly's Roll — a printed book of 1898 — gives the same day, and has until now been the only authority for it.
The funeral, which nobody here knew about

The Kent Herald of 24 May: he “was interred at Chatham WITH MILITARY HONOURS” on the Saturday. That Saturday was 19 May 1827 — the exact date of entry 1571 in Chatham St Mary the Virgin's burial register. A local paper and a parish clerk, independently.
The Kent Herald says “at an advanced age”. The register says seventy-six.

Seventeen notices in England, Ireland and Scotland — London, Canterbury, Windsor, Oxford, Perth, Dublin, Limerick, Clonmel, Drogheda, Boyle. A Major-General of Engineers was national news for a fortnight.

withholds.head: Not one of the seventeen gives him a forename.
withholds.body: Every single notice reads “Major-General D'Arcy” and stops. No Robert. No father, no seat, no county, no “son of”, no “of —— Hall”. The press of 1827 was fluent in exactly that grammar — on the same pages he shares, men are “only son of Mr. John Blades, of Ludgate-hill”, “fourth daughter of Charles Coleman, Esq.”, “of Denne Hill, Kent, aged 84”. He gets a rank and a place of death.
withholds.means: This was the most promising unopened door to Robert D'Arcy's parentage, and it is now open and empty. Seventeen contemporary notices in three countries name nobody he was related to. That is not a gap in the archive; it is a fact about the man, and it points the same way everything else has: he was an officer who rose on service, not a family the papers felt obliged to place.
